course.title: Systems Programming: Memory, Operating Systems, C and Rust
course.description: See how a program really uses memory, the operating system and the processor, and learn why Rust's ownership rules exist by first meeting the C faults they prevent.
course.audience: Someone who has written small programs in Rust, knows variables, types and functions, and wants to understand what happens underneath: bytes, stacks, processes, threads, virtual memory, caches and the C boundary. No operating systems background is assumed. Rust Foundations is expected to cover enough syntax (let, functions, structs, Vec, String, println!) before lesson 1; this course teaches ownership and borrowing from first principles.

paragraphs: A Rust program can be correct on paper and still surprise you, because every value in it lives in some particular place, and the place decides what the program costs and what it is allowed to do. A four-byte integer occupies four consecutive bytes in an order the machine chose, a struct leaves gaps so that its fields start where the processor likes them, and a Vec keeps a small handle on the stack that points at a buffer on the heap. Systems programming is the study of those places, and of the operating system and the hardware that provide them.

The same view explains why Rust is built as it is. In C, a pointer can outlive the memory it points to, a buffer can be written past its end, and the same block can be freed twice, all without a word from the compiler. Rust's rules about ownership and borrowing exist to rule out faults like these, and once you have met the fault, each rule reads as the compiler checking something that C leaves to the programmer.

The places a value can live extend beyond the program itself. The operating system gives each process its own address space and its own table of open files, and a program asks it for anything outside that space through a system call. The processor, for its part, keeps recently used memory in small caches, so the order in which a program touches its data changes how fast it runs. Most of this can be worked out with arithmetic on paper, which lets you say how a piece of code will behave, and why, before you run it.
outcomes: You'll be able to predict how a fixed-width integer, a struct or a Vec is laid out in memory.
You'll be able to explain a Rust ownership or borrow error and fix it.
You'll be able to read short C fragments and name the memory fault they contain.
You'll be able to explain what a process, a file descriptor, a thread and a system call are, and count the effects of fork.
You'll be able to compute average turnaround for a schedule, translate a virtual address and count cache misses.
You'll be able to say what unsafe allows and call a C function from Rust.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Rust Foundations, How Computers Solve Problems.

modules.title: Memory, from bytes to ownership
modules.description: How values sit in memory, where they live, and how Rust and C decide when memory is released.

modules.title: Processes and the operating system
modules.description: What the kernel gives a running program: processes, files, threads and a share of the processor.

modules.title: Memory hardware and the boundary
modules.description: Virtual memory, caches, and the line where safe Rust meets C.

concepts.title: Byte and address
concepts.summary: Memory is a sequence of bytes, each with a numeric address, and every larger value is stored as consecutive bytes.

concepts.title: Two's complement
concepts.summary: A signed n-bit integer reuses the same bit patterns as an unsigned one, treating a pattern with the top bit set as its value minus 2^n.

concepts.title: Endianness
concepts.summary: Little-endian machines store the least significant byte of a multi-byte integer at the lowest address.

concepts.title: Alignment
concepts.summary: A value of alignment a must start at an address that is a multiple of a, and primitive types are usually aligned to their own size.

concepts.title: Padding
concepts.summary: The compiler inserts unused bytes between fields so that each field lands on an aligned offset and the struct size is a multiple of its alignment.

concepts.title: repr(C)
concepts.summary: The repr(C) attribute fixes field order to declaration order so the layout matches what a C compiler would produce.

concepts.title: Stack frame
concepts.summary: Each function call gets a frame holding its locals, and the frame disappears when the function returns.

concepts.title: Heap
concepts.summary: The heap holds allocations whose size or lifetime is not fixed at compile time, obtained and released explicitly or through an owner type.

concepts.title: Handle and buffer
concepts.summary: A Vec, String or Box is a small fixed-size handle on the stack that points at a buffer on the heap.

concepts.title: Owner
concepts.summary: Every value has exactly one owner, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped.

concepts.title: Move
concepts.summary: Assigning or passing a value that owns heap data transfers ownership and leaves the source unusable.

concepts.title: Drop
concepts.summary: Dropping a value runs its destructor and frees what it owns, and locals drop in reverse order of declaration.

concepts.title: Borrow
concepts.summary: A reference lets code use a value without owning it, and the compiler checks that the owner outlives every reference.

concepts.title: Shared XOR mutable
concepts.summary: At any moment a value has either any number of shared references or exactly one mutable reference.

concepts.title: Lifetime
concepts.summary: A lifetime names how long a reference stays valid, and a signature relates the lifetimes of inputs to the output.

concepts.title: Pointer
concepts.summary: A pointer is a variable holding an address, and adding n to a typed pointer moves it by n times the size of the pointed-to type.

concepts.title: Array decay
concepts.summary: In most expressions and in function parameters an array name becomes a pointer to its first element, so sizeof no longer sees the array length.

concepts.title: Undefined behaviour
concepts.summary: The C standard places no requirement on a program that frees memory twice, reads freed memory, or indexes outside an object.

concepts.title: Process
concepts.summary: A process is a running program with its own virtual address space, file descriptors and identity, scheduled by the kernel.

concepts.title: System call
concepts.summary: A system call is the controlled entry that lets user code ask the kernel to act, switching the processor from user mode to kernel mode and back.

concepts.title: fork and exec
concepts.summary: fork creates a near-copy of the calling process, returning 0 in the child and the child's pid in the parent, and exec replaces the current program with another.

concepts.title: File descriptor
concepts.summary: A file descriptor is a small integer that indexes a per-process table of open files, pipes and sockets.

concepts.title: Lowest unused descriptor
concepts.summary: open returns the smallest descriptor number not currently in use, which is how redirection works.

concepts.title: Stdio buffer
concepts.summary: C's stdio collects output in a user-space buffer and calls write only when the buffer fills, a newline arrives on a terminal, or the program flushes or exits.

concepts.title: Thread
concepts.summary: A thread is an independent flow of execution inside a process, sharing the process's address space with its siblings.

concepts.title: Data race
concepts.summary: A data race occurs when two threads access the same location at once, at least one writes, and nothing orders the accesses.

concepts.title: Arc and Mutex
concepts.summary: Arc gives shared ownership across threads, and Mutex allows only the holder of its lock to reach the data inside.

concepts.title: Turnaround time
concepts.summary: A job's turnaround time is its completion time minus its arrival time.

concepts.title: Round robin
concepts.summary: Round robin gives each runnable job a fixed time slice in turn, then puts it at the back of the queue.

concepts.title: Deadlock
concepts.summary: A deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and a circular wait, and removing any one prevents it.

concepts.title: Virtual address
concepts.summary: A virtual address is what a process uses; hardware translates it to a physical address, so each process sees its own private space.

concepts.title: Page table
concepts.summary: A page table maps each virtual page number to a physical frame, and the offset within the page is carried over unchanged.

concepts.title: TLB
concepts.summary: The translation lookaside buffer caches recent page translations so that most accesses skip the page table in memory.

concepts.title: Cache line
concepts.summary: Memory moves between levels in fixed blocks, typically 64 bytes, so reading one byte loads its whole line.

concepts.title: Locality
concepts.summary: Programs that reuse recent data (temporal) or touch nearby addresses (spatial) hit the cache more often.

concepts.title: Row-major layout
concepts.summary: A row-major array stores each row contiguously, so walking along a row touches consecutive addresses and walking down a column jumps by the row length.

concepts.title: Unsafe block
concepts.summary: An unsafe block does not switch checks off; it lets the programmer use five extra operations and promises the compiler that the surrounding code upholds their conditions.

concepts.title: Raw pointer
concepts.summary: A raw pointer (*const T or *mut T) carries an address without ownership or lifetime, and dereferencing it requires unsafe.

concepts.title: Foreign function interface
concepts.summary: Calling C from Rust needs an extern declaration, C-compatible types and layout, and a promise that the C function meets the stated contract.

lessons.title: Bytes, integers and overflow

lead.text: Each box in memory holds eight binary digits, and eight bits can be set in 2^8 = 256 different patterns, so a single box holds one number from 0 to 255. Such a box is a **byte**, and its position in the row is its **address**, which is itself just a number: the byte at address 0x1000 is followed by the byte at 0x1001, and so on. A value larger than 255, such as 258, is stored across several consecutive bytes, which is why the opening example needed four of them.

Writing a byte as eight binary digits is exact but tiring to read, so programmers group the bits in fours. Four bits can be set in sixteen patterns, and **hexadecimal**, or base 16, gives each pattern one digit: the digits 0 to 9, followed by A to F for ten to fifteen. A byte is therefore always exactly two hex digits, and the prefix `0x` marks a number as hex. The figure shows the byte 10110111 in both forms.

afterFigure.text: The leftmost bit of a byte is worth 128 and each bit to its right is worth half of the one before, so 10110111 is 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 + 1, which is 183. Hex reaches the same answer faster. The left four bits 1011 are eleven, which is the digit B, and the right four bits 0111 are seven, so the byte is 0xB7, and 11 × 16 + 7 is again 183. **To convert hex to decimal, multiply each digit by its place value and add**, where a two-digit number has place values 16 and 1 and a three-digit number has 256, 16 and 1.

diagram.alt: A byte drawn as eight bit boxes holding 10110111 with place values 128 down to 1, then grouped into two sets of four bits that are the hex digits B and 7.
diagram.caption: The byte 10110111 in binary and in hex. Both readings give 183. Use the buttons to switch.

reveal.text: The opening example, 258, is 0x102 by the same method, because 1 × 256 + 0 × 16 + 2 = 258. Padded to the four bytes of a `u32`, it is 0x00000102.

lead.text: Rust names the width of every integer type: `u8` and `i8` use one byte, `u16` and `i16` two, `u32` and `i32` four, and `u64` and `i64` eight. A width of n bits has 2^n patterns, so an **unsigned** type, written with a u, reads them as the numbers 0 up to 2^n − 1, and a `u8` therefore runs from 0 to 255. A **signed** type, written with an i, has to give some of its patterns to negative numbers, and the split is even: it runs from -2^(n-1) up to 2^(n-1) − 1, which for an `i8` is -128 to 127.
The figure uses three bits, so that all eight patterns fit on one row.

afterFigure.text: Read as unsigned, the patterns count from 0 up to 7. Read as signed, the first four keep their values 0 to 3 and the last four become -4 to -1. **The patterns do not change; only the numbers assigned to them do.** The machine stores nothing but the pattern, and the type, `u8` or `i8`, tells the compiler which reading to apply.

diagram.alt: Eight boxes holding the 3-bit patterns 000 to 111. Read as unsigned they stand for 0 to 7. Read as signed the last four stand for minus 4 to minus 1.
diagram.caption: The patterns never change. Only the numbers assigned to them do. Use the buttons to switch the reading.

reveal.text: The same rule gives -32768 as the smallest i16, one further from zero than the largest, because zero uses up one of the non-negative patterns.

lead.text: The way of assigning the signed readings in the figure on the screen before last is called **two's complement**, and its rule is short. If the top bit of a pattern is 0, the number is the unsigned value, exactly as before. If the top bit is 1, the number is the unsigned value *minus* 2^n, where n is the width. The pattern 11111111 is 255 as a `u8`, so as an `i8` it is 255 − 256 = -1, and the pattern 11111010 is 250 as a `u8` and 250 − 256 = -6 as an `i8`.

The scheme was adopted because addition needs no special case for negative numbers. Adding the patterns for 6 and -6 as ordinary unsigned numbers gives 00000110 + 11111010 = 100000000, a nine-bit result whose top bit does not fit in a byte, and the eight bits that remain are 00000000, which is zero. To write -6 yourself, invert every bit of 6 and add one: 00000110 inverts to 11111001, and adding one gives 11111010.

steps.headline: Read the pattern 11111011 as an i8, and then check the result.

workedSteps.text: Work out the pattern as an unsigned number first, using the place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1.
The top bit is 1, so the signed value is the unsigned value minus 2^8 = 256.
To check, invert the pattern, which gives 00000100, and add one. Read the result in decimal.

steps.headline: Read 200u8 as an i8, using the same steps.

workedSteps.text: 200 as an unsigned number is the pattern 11001000, because 128 + 64 + 8 = 200.
The top bit is 1, so the signed value subtracts 256 from the unsigned value.
Work out the result.

lead.text: A `u32` needs four bytes, and there are two sensible orders in which to put them. The number 258 is 0x00000102, whose *most* significant byte, the one worth the most, is 00, and whose *least* significant byte is 02. A **little-endian** machine stores the least significant byte at the lowest address, so 258 appears in memory as 02 01 00 00, whereas a **big-endian** machine stores the most significant byte first, as 00 00 01 02. Network protocols have traditionally used big-endian order, and the processors in most laptops, phones and servers, x86 and the usual ARM configuration, are little-endian.

afterFigure.text: In Rust, `258u32.to_le_bytes()` returns `[2, 1, 0, 0]` and `258u32.to_be_bytes()` returns `[0, 0, 1, 2]`, while `to_ne_bytes` gives whichever order the machine itself uses. The common mistake is to read the little-endian bytes from left to right as though they were the number: the bytes 02 01 00 00 are not 0x02010000. Read from the highest address down to the lowest they give 00 00 01 02, and that is the number.

diagram.alt: Four memory boxes at addresses 0x1000 to 0x1003. Little-endian holds 02 01 00 00 for the number 258. Big-endian holds 00 00 01 02.

reveal.text: The bytes in memory are 04 03 02 01. A big-endian machine would hold the same number as 01 02 03 04, so the same question has a different answer there.
The counter reaches 255 after five steps and the sixth step returns it to 0, so ten steps from 250 end at 4. The next screen explains all four methods.

lead.text: When the true result of an arithmetic operation does not fit in the type, the operation **overflows**. A plain `a + b` in Rust makes a choice that you did not write: a debug build panics, which stops the program with an error message, while a release build wraps around unless overflow checks have been switched on. The same source therefore behaves differently depending on how it was built, and the standard library offers four methods whose meaning is the same in every build.

**wrapping_add** keeps only the low bits, which is the result modulo 256 for a `u8`. **saturating_add** stops at the largest value the type can hold. **checked_add** returns `None` when the result does not fit and `Some(result)` when it does. **overflowing_add** returns the wrapped result together with a flag that says whether wrapping happened.

afterFigure.text: The figure adds 100 to a `u8` holding 200. The true result, 300, does not fit, so `wrapping_add` returns 300 − 256 = 44, `saturating_add` returns 255, `checked_add` returns `None`, and `overflowing_add` returns `(44, true)`. C treats the same mistake very differently: overflow of a *signed* integer is undefined behaviour, which means the language places no requirement at all on what the program then does, and a later lesson returns to that.

reveal.text: The None case forces the caller to deal with the failure, because an Option must be unpacked before its number can be used.
127 is 01111111, and adding one gives 10000000, whose set top bit makes it 128 − 256 = -128. Wrapping in a signed type therefore jumps from the largest value to the smallest.

lessons.orientation: Read bytes, hex, signed integers and byte order, and predict what each of Rust's overflow methods returns.
lessons.nextAction: Compute where each field of a struct sits in memory, and why the compiler leaves gaps between them.

blocks.text: The Rust statement `let x: u32 = 258;` puts a number in memory, which is a long row of numbered boxes that can each hold a single value from 0 to 255. Because 258 is too large for one box, a `u32` takes four consecutive boxes, and they contain 2, 1, 0 and 0, with the 2 first. The number exists in memory only as those four small values, and what it means depends on their order and on the type used to read them.

Knowing how the boxes are filled lets you read the bytes of any integer and say what the same pattern means as a signed or an unsigned number. It also lets you predict what an addition does when its result is too big for the boxes it was given, a case with more than one possible outcome in Rust, since the program can panic, wrap around, stop at the largest value or report the problem, and the programmer has to choose which.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to convert between hex, binary and decimal, read a bit pattern as signed or unsigned, say which byte comes first in memory, and predict what each overflow method returns.
intro.whyItMatters: Every layout, pointer and cache question later in the course starts from knowing which bytes a value occupies.

recap.keyIdea: A value in memory is a pattern of bytes, and its type decides whether those bytes are read as signed or unsigned, in which order, and what happens when arithmetic outruns them.

blocks.text: A byte holds one of 256 patterns, hex writes it in two digits, and a signed type reads a pattern whose top bit is set as the unsigned value minus 2^n. A u32 occupies four consecutive bytes, with the least significant byte first on a little-endian machine.

When arithmetic produces a result that does not fit, the four methods `wrapping_add`, `saturating_add`, `checked_add` and `overflowing_add` make the outcome explicit, whereas the plain operator panics in a debug build and wraps in a release build.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson places several values side by side in one struct and asks why the compiler leaves gaps between them.

lessons.title: Layout, size and alignment

lead.text: A processor does not fetch memory one byte at a time. It loads aligned chunks, and a four-byte value that sits inside one chunk arrives in a single load, whereas a value that straddles the boundary between two chunks needs two loads and some shifting to be put together. On some processors a misaligned load is not allowed at all and faults. The remedy built into every compiler is a rule: a type has an **alignment**, and a value of that type must start at an address that is a multiple of it.

For the primitive types on a typical 64-bit machine the alignment equals the size, so a u8 has alignment 1, a u16 has 2, a u32 has 4 and a u64 has 8. The figure shows the same four-byte value at address 4, which is a multiple of 4, and at address 6, which is not.

afterFigure.text: At address 4 the value fills exactly one word. At address 6 it covers the last two bytes of one word and the first two of the next, which is the layout the alignment rule forbids. The rule costs some space, as the next screens show, and **that space is the price paid for loads that stay fast and legal**.

reveal.text: Rounding up in this way is the operation the compiler performs between every pair of fields, so the same arithmetic reappears on the next screen.

lead.text: Consider a [[struct|A group of named fields stored together. Met in Rust Foundations.]] with a `u8` field `a` followed by a `u32` field `b`. The field `a` takes byte 0. The next free byte is 1, but `b` has alignment 4, so it cannot start there, and the compiler skips to offset 4. The skipped bytes 1, 2 and 3 are **padding**: they belong to the struct and hold nothing. The field `b` then fills bytes 4 to 7, and the struct is 8 bytes long although its fields hold only 5.

A struct has an alignment of its own, which is the largest alignment among its fields, so this one has alignment 4, and its size must be a multiple of that. The reason is that a row of such structs, an array, needs every element to start aligned. The figure puts b first to show the second kind of padding: the fields then end at byte 5, and bytes 5 to 7 are added at the end.

afterFigure.text: Both orders give a size of 8 here, but they arrive at it differently, with the padding in the middle in one case and at the end in the other. Rust's attribute **#[repr(C)]**, which lays fields out in declaration order exactly as a C compiler would, is what these examples assume, because plain Rust is free to choose another order.

ends at 5, but the size is rounded up to 8: bytes 5 to 7 are padding</text><text class="t-bold t-accent" x="320" y="255" text-anchor="middle">struct size 8, alignment 4</text></svg>

lead.text: Every layout in this lesson follows from one operation, rounding up to a multiple. Written as `round_up(x, a)`, it gives the smallest multiple of a that is at least x, so `round_up(5, 4)` is 8, `round_up(8, 8)` is 8, because 8 is already a multiple, and `round_up(13, 8)` is 16.

With that, the layout rule has three parts. Each field starts at round_up(end of the previous field, the field's alignment). The struct's alignment is the largest field alignment. The size is round_up(end of the last field, the struct's alignment). The first field always starts at offset 0, and no part of the rule ever moves a field earlier than the order in which it was declared.

steps.headline: Lay out #[repr(C)] struct S { a: u8, b: u32, c: u8 } and find its size.

workedSteps.text: The field a is a u8, so it starts at offset 0 and ends at 1.
The field `b` is a `u32`, so it starts at `round_up(1, 4)` = 4 and ends at 8.
The field c is a u8 with alignment 1, so it starts directly at 8 and ends at 9.
The struct's alignment is 4, the largest among its fields. Work out the size, which is `round_up(9, 4)`.

steps.headline: Lay out #[repr(C)] struct U { a: u8, b: u16, c: u64 } and find where c starts.

workedSteps.text: The field a starts at offset 0 and ends at 1.
The field `b` is a `u16`, so it starts at `round_up(1, 2)` = 2 and ends at 4.
The field c is a u64. Work out its byte offset.

reveal.text: Both u8 fields fit in the first four bytes, so only two bytes of padding remain before b, and the struct is smaller than the one in the worked example.

lead.text: The worked example needed 12 bytes for six bytes of data, and the same fields declared as a, c, b needed 8. Alignment is always a power of two, so putting fields in order of decreasing alignment leaves no gap between them, and the only padding left is at the end. That is why reordering can shrink a struct, and why a library that must keep a fixed order, as one that matches a C header does, pays for padding that a free order would avoid.

You do not have to compute these sizes by hand. `std::mem::size_of` and `std::mem::align_of` report them, and the macro `offset_of!` reports where a field starts. The figure prints the sizes of three structs built from the same three fields.

afterFigure.text: The first two lines agree with the hand calculations: 12 for the order `a`, `b`, `c` and 8 for `a`, `c`, `b`. The third struct has no `repr(C)`, so Rust may choose the order, and the compiler used here chose one that gives 8. The language does not promise that order, which is exactly why `repr(C)` exists for code that must match another language's layout.

outcome.stdout:
repr(C) a, b, c: 12
repr(C) a, c, b: 8
plain Rust a, b, c: 8

reveal.text: Reordering saved eight bytes here, which is a third of the original 24. Sorting the fields by decreasing alignment will not always shrink a struct, but it never makes one larger.
Here the padding is a single byte between b and c, and the end of c at offset 8 is already a multiple of 4, so nothing is added at the end.

lessons.orientation: Work out where each field of a struct sits in memory, how much padding the compiler adds, and why field order changes the size.
lessons.nextAction: See where values live while a program runs: the stack, which holds fixed-size values, and the heap, which holds the rest.

blocks.text: The `struct { a: u8, b: u32 }` has a one-byte field and a four-byte field, so its data adds up to five bytes, yet Rust reports its size as eight. The three extra bytes are inserted by the compiler after `a`, so that `b` starts at an address divisible by four, which is where a processor can load a four-byte value in a single step.

The gap follows from a rule that is simple enough to apply on paper. Applied to any struct, it gives the size, and so the memory a million of them occupy, and it shows why swapping two field declarations can shrink a struct without removing any data.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the offset of each field and the size of a #[repr(C)] struct, say why padding exists, and reorder fields to shrink a struct.
intro.whyItMatters: Struct layout decides how much memory a program uses and how data crosses into C.

recap.keyIdea: A struct places each field at a multiple of its alignment and rounds its size up to its own alignment, so padding appears and field order can change the size.

blocks.text: Every value has an alignment, usually its own size for primitive types, and a field starts at the end of the previous one rounded up to that alignment. The struct as a whole is rounded up to its largest field alignment, which adds padding at the end.

Padding is the price of loads that stay fast and legal, and declaring the largest fields first usually keeps it small. With `repr(C)` the order is the one written, and without it Rust may choose another.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks where a value lives once it is laid out, and why a value of unknown size cannot live in the place that fixed-size values do.

lessons.title: The stack and the heap

lead.text: When a function is called, the program sets aside a block of memory for it, the function's **stack frame**, which holds its parameters, its local variables and the place to return to. When the function returns, the block is released at once. Because the last function called is always the first to return, the frames form a **stack**: new ones go on top, and only the top one is removed.
The figure follows the program in the opener. main calls f with 3, and f calls g with 4. At the moment g runs, three frames exist, one for each function that has been called and has not yet finished.

afterFigure.text: Each frame holds only the names of its own function, so two calls of the same function get separate frames with separate variables. When `g` returns, its frame disappears and `f`'s frame is on top again, with the value `g` produced ready to use. **Setting aside and releasing a frame is nothing more than moving one pointer**, which is why the stack is quick.

diagram.alt: A stack of boxes for the frames of main, f and g. The boxes stack up as each function is called, and the top one is the running function. When g returns its box is removed.
diagram.caption: Frames pile up as calls are made, and the top frame belongs to the function that is running. Use the buttons to step through.

reveal.text: When g returns, two frames are left, and when f returns, only main's frame remains. The frames disappear in exactly the reverse order from the one in which they were made.

lead.text: The compiler decides how large each frame is before the program runs, because making room for a call has to be one quick adjustment. This works for an i32, a struct or an array of four numbers, whose sizes are fixed by their types. It cannot work for the text a user types or a list that grows during a run, because nobody knows in advance how much room they need.

That kind of value lives on the **heap**, a region from which the program asks for a block of whatever size it needs while it is running, and to which it later gives the block back. The component that hands out blocks is the *allocator*, and it has to find a free block of the right size, which costs more than moving a pointer. The stack is not magic, however, and the heap is not slow in any absolute sense: the stack is simply cheaper per request, and the heap is the only choice when the size is not fixed or the value must outlive the function that made it.

reveal.text: The word for it comes from the way the frames pile up, last in and first out.

lead.text: A `Vec<i32>` has to hold any number of elements, so what it keeps on the stack is only a **handle** made of three 8-byte words on a 64-bit machine: a pointer to the buffer on the heap, the buffer's **capacity**, which is how many elements it has room for, and the **length**, which is how many it holds at present. The elements themselves, the numbers 10, 20 and 30 in the figure, sit in the heap buffer, next to each other.

A `String` is built in the same way, with its text as bytes in the buffer, and a `Box<i32>` is simpler still, a single pointer to one `i32` on the heap, so it is 8 bytes. A `&str` is only a pointer and a length, because it *borrows* text that somebody else owns and has no capacity to record.

afterFigure.text: Rust can report these sizes for you with `std::mem::size_of`, so `size_of::<Box<i32>>()` gives 8, and for a `Vec` or a `String` it gives the size of the three-word handle. **The handle is the same size whether the Vec holds three elements or three million**, because the elements are not in it.

reveal.text: The new capacity is 8, double the old one. Growing a full buffer by one slot would mean copying all the elements on every push, so the library makes room for several more pushes at once.

lead.text: The elements of a Vec must sit next to each other, because that is what makes indexing a single addition. A full buffer cannot simply be extended, since the memory that follows it may be in use by something else, so the Vec asks the allocator for a new, larger buffer, copies every element into it, updates the pointer and capacity in its handle, and hands the old buffer back. The figure shows the three stages for a Vec with room for four elements.

The standard library currently doubles the capacity each time, so a Vec started empty reports capacity 4 and then 8 as it grows, which means most pushes cost nothing extra and the copying happens now and then. The exact growth rule is not promised by the documentation, only that pushing is cheap on average.

afterFigure.text: This also explains a surprise for the unwary: a pointer into the old buffer is left pointing at memory that has been given back, and the next lessons show how Rust makes such a pointer impossible to use.

workedSteps.text: The text hello is 5 bytes, so the String needs a heap buffer for those 5 bytes, and its length and capacity are both 5.
The handle that stands for s lives in the frame of the function that declared it, and it holds the pointer to the buffer and the two counts.
Work out the size of the handle: three words of 8 bytes each.

reveal.text: The old buffer is freed after the copy, so the Vec never holds two buffers for long.

steps.headline: Start with Vec::new() for i32 and push nine values, noting the capacity after each push.

workedSteps.text: After the first push the library allocates room for 4, so the capacity is 4 and stays 4 through the fourth push.
The fifth push finds the buffer full and doubles it.
The ninth push finds the buffer full again. Work out the capacity afterwards.

reveal.text: A pointer says where the text starts and a length says where it ends. Nothing owned means nothing to resize, so no capacity is needed.

lessons.orientation: Decide whether a value lives on the stack or the heap, and say what happens in memory when a Vec grows.
lessons.nextAction: Use these regions to explain who owns a value, when it moves and when its memory is released.

blocks.text: In a program where main calls f and f calls g, the processor has to keep the variables of every call and remember where each call returns to. It does both in one region of memory that grows by a fixed amount at every call and shrinks by the same amount at every return, which makes it one of the cheapest things a program does.

That arrangement works only because the amount is known before the program runs. A value whose size is decided during a run, such as the text a user types, needs a second region that hands out blocks of whatever size is asked for, at a higher cost for each request. A Vec keeps a small fixed-size part in the first region and its elements in the second, and seeing how the two fit together explains what happens when its buffer fills up.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say where a value lives, state the size of a Vec's or String's handle, and trace what a Vec does when it is full.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every ownership rule in Rust is about the heap buffers that handles point to.

recap.keyIdea: Fixed-size values live in stack frames that come and go with calls, and values whose size is decided at run time live on the heap behind a fixed-size handle.

blocks.text: A call adds a frame to the stack and a return removes it, which is only a pointer movement. A Vec or String keeps a handle of pointer, capacity and length in its frame, and its elements or text in a heap buffer.
When a push finds the buffer full, the Vec allocates a larger one, copies the elements across and frees the old one, so the handle stays the same size while the buffer changes.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks who is responsible for freeing a heap buffer, and gives Rust's answer: exactly one owner.

lessons.title: Ownership, moves and drop

lead.text: The previous lesson ended with a `Vec` or a `String` as a handle on the stack pointing to a buffer on the heap, which raises the question of who gives the buffer back. If copying the handle produced a second handle with an equal right to free the buffer, the buffer would be freed twice, and freeing the same block twice corrupts the allocator's records. Rust avoids this with a rule: each value has exactly one **owner**, which is the variable that holds it.

When the owner goes out of scope, which for a local variable means reaching the closing brace of the block that declares it, Rust **drops** the value, running its cleanup and releasing the buffer. The point of the drop is fixed by the shape of the program, so it is the same on every run and no collector ever has to search for garbage.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the fault the rule prevents. When two handles both think they own the buffer, each one frees it as it goes away, and the second free acts on memory that has already been returned.

diagram.alt: A stack column with two handles, a and b, both with arrows to one heap buffer holding x. In the second view the buffer is marked as freed twice, which is the fault ownership prevents.

lead.text: The assignment `let b = a` copies the handle from `a` to `b`, so `b` now holds the pointer, the capacity and the length. The buffer on the heap is not touched. To keep a single owner, Rust then treats `a` as empty: the value has **moved** to `b`, and the name `a` may not be used again unless it is given a new value.
Passing a value to a function is a move in the same way. The parameter becomes the new owner, and the caller's variable is invalid afterwards.

afterFigure.text: Moving is cheap, since the cost is the size of the handle whatever the length of the text, and it is safe, since there is never more than one owner to free the buffer. The figure shows the two stages, with the original handle drawn dashed once it has given up its value.

lead.text: When a program uses a moved value, rustc reports error E0382 and marks three places. The first is the declaration, with a note that the value has a type, here `String`, that does not implement the **Copy** trait, which explains why assigning it moves it instead of copying it. The second is the line where the value moved, and the third is the later line that tried to use it.

The figure passes the String to a function and then prints it. The move happens at the call, because the parameter of consume takes ownership, and the compiler suggests two repairs: change the parameter to borrow the value, which the next lesson explains, or clone the value if two copies are really wanted.

afterFigure.text: Read the marked lines in order, declaration, move, use, and the fault is usually clear at once. The error is not about memory being unsafe at that moment. It is the compiler refusing to accept a program in which a name could outlive its value.

lead.text: Within one scope, locals are dropped in the reverse of the order in which they were declared, so a value that was created later, and may depend on an earlier one, is cleaned up first. A value moved into a function belongs to that function's parameter, so it is dropped when the function returns, even though the caller declared it.

In the figure, main creates a, b and then moves a into consume. The function prints a line, and its parameter is dropped as it finishes, so drop a appears before main prints its own end. The value b, which never moved, is dropped when main finishes.

afterFigure.text: The caller cannot drop `a` a second time, since it no longer owns it, and that is the single-owner rule at work again. **Whoever owns a value when its scope ends is the one that drops it.**

lead.text: When two separate copies are really wanted, the clone method makes one: it allocates a new buffer, copies the text into it and returns a new String that owns that buffer, so both the original and the copy remain valid. Cloning costs an allocation and a copy that grows with the length of the text, so it is the right answer when a second owner is needed and a poor one when the code only needs to look at the value.

Types whose whole value is small and lives on the stack are different. An `i32` has no buffer to free, so a copy of it is as good as the original, and such types are marked **Copy**: assigning one copies it, and the original stays usable. The figure shows a clone of a `String` and a copy of an `i32`.

The second line moves the handle to b. Nothing is allocated, a is no longer valid, and b owns the same single buffer.
The third line clones b. Work out how many buffers exist afterwards.

lessons.orientation: Predict when a Rust value moves, when it is dropped, and which compiler error follows a use after a move.
lessons.nextAction: Look at a value without taking it, using borrows, and meet the rules that keep a borrow from outliving its value.

blocks.text: A String is a handle of three words on the stack that points to a buffer on the heap, so copying the handle byte for byte would leave two variables pointing at one buffer. When both went out of scope, each would free it, and the same block would be returned to the allocator twice. In C this is a classic fault known as a double free, and it damages the records the allocator keeps about which blocks are free, often long before the program visibly fails.

Rust rules the fault out by giving every buffer a single owner, the one variable responsible for freeing it. With that rule you can follow a program line by line and say which variable owns each value, what an assignment or a function call does to it, and when it is freed.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say when a value moves, predict the order in which values are dropped, read error E0382, and choose between a clone and a move.
intro.whyItMatters: Ownership is the rule behind most of the compiler errors you will meet in Rust.

recap.keyIdea: Each value has one owner, assignment and calls move it, and the value is dropped when its owner goes out of scope.

blocks.text: A move copies only the handle and leaves the buffer where it is, after which the old name is invalid, and the compiler reports a later use as E0382. Locals are dropped in reverse declaration order, and a value moved into a function is dropped where its new owner ends.
Clone makes an independent copy at the cost of an allocation, while Copy types such as i32 are duplicated freely because they own nothing on the heap.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows how to use a value without owning it, by borrowing it, and what the compiler requires of a borrow.

lessons.title: Borrowing and lifetimes

lead.text: The previous lesson showed that handing a String to a function moves it, which is awkward when the function only needs to look at the text. The alternative is to *borrow* the value. Writing `&a` creates a **reference** to `a`, an address that the function can read through, and the function's parameter has the type `&String` instead of `String`. The owner stays the owner: the reference neither frees the buffer nor prevents the caller from using `a` again afterwards.

A reference of this kind is a **shared borrow**, and any number of them may exist at once, because reading does not interfere with reading. A **mutable borrow**, written `&mut a`, allows the holder to change the value. The figure passes `&a` to a function and then prints `a`, which a move would have forbidden.

afterFigure.text: The word borrow is accurate: the reference is lent for a while and the owner has the value back when the borrow ends. What remains to be settled is how long a borrow may last and what the owner may do meanwhile, and that is the subject of the rest of this lesson.

reveal.text: The push needs mutable access while f, a shared borrow, is going to be used on the next line, so the compiler reports E0502 and marks the three lines involved.

lead.text: In C a program can hold a pointer to the first element of an array and then call a function that grows the array. If the array has to move to a larger block, the old block is freed, and the pointer is left pointing at memory that no longer belongs to the array. A pointer of this kind is **dangling**, and using it is a fault the C compiler does not detect. The figure shows the same thing with a Rust `Vec`, where `f` stands for a reference into the buffer and a push makes the buffer move.

Rust's rule closes this gap. At any moment a value may have **many shared borrows, or exactly one mutable borrow, but never both**. A push needs mutable access to the `Vec`, so it cannot happen while a shared reference into the `Vec` is still going to be used, and the reference can never be found pointing at a freed buffer.

afterFigure.text: The rule is often described as a defence against threads, and it does serve that purpose, but the Vec example needs no threads at all. The danger is any holder of a reference being surprised by a change made through a different name, and the rule removes the surprise by making such a change impossible while the reference lives.

lead.text: Each code names one way of breaking the rules. E0502 appears when a mutable borrow is taken while a shared one is still going to be used, as in the Vec example. E0499 appears when a second mutable borrow is taken while the first is still going to be used. E0597 appears when a reference is kept after the value it points to has been dropped, which the compiler words as the value not living long enough.

The figure shows E0597. The variable `x` is declared in an inner block and is dropped at the closing brace, but `r`, declared outside the block, still refers to it, and the later `println!` would read the freed value. The message marks four places: where `x` is declared, where the borrow is taken, where `x` is dropped while still borrowed, and where the borrow is used afterwards.

afterFigure.text: Reading the labelled spans in order tells you which of the three rules applies and where to look for the repair. The usual repairs are to end the borrow earlier, to give the value a longer scope, or, where two owners are really needed, to clone.

reveal.text: The same exclusivity is what lets a mutable borrow change the value safely: nobody else holds a way to see it half changed.

lead.text: Consider a function that takes two string slices and returns the longer one. Its result is a reference, and a reference is only valid while the value it points to is alive, so the compiler has to know which input the result borrows from. The body shows that it could be either, since one branch returns a and the other returns b, and the signature does not say.

The compiler therefore stops at the signature, with error E0106, missing lifetime specifier. The message says that the return type contains a borrowed value, but the signature does not say whether it is borrowed from a or b. It also shows the repair, in which each reference gets a name written with an apostrophe, such as 'a.

afterFigure.text: A **lifetime** is the stretch of the program during which a reference is valid, and naming one lets a signature talk about it. The next screen shows what the name promises.

outcome.diagnostics:
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
 --> main.rs:1:33
  |
1 | fn longest(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str {
  |               ----     ----     ^ expected named lifetime parameter
  |
  = help: this function's return type contains a borrowed value, but the signature does not say whether it is borrowed from `a` or `b`
help: consider introducing a named lifetime parameter
  |
1 | fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
  |           ++++     ++          ++          ++

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0106`.

lead.text: The repaired signature is `fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str`. It declares a lifetime named `'a` and gives it to both inputs and to the result, which says that the result cannot outlive either input. This changes nothing about how long any value lives, since values are still dropped when their owners' scopes end. It records a relationship, and the compiler checks that every caller respects it.

In the figure, the repaired function is called with a String that lives to the end of main and another that lives only inside an inner block. The call itself is accepted, but the result is used after the block, when b has been dropped, so the compiler reports E0597 at that line. The same function called with two values that both outlive the use compiles and prints pear.

afterFigure.text: The practical rule is that the result is valid for the *shorter* of the two spans, because it might refer to either one. If you ever need a result that refers only to the first input, give that input the name and leave the other unnamed.

reveal.text: The reference f is last used on the print line, so its borrow has ended by the push, and the compiler accepts the program.

lead.text: It would be natural to expect a reference to be alive until the closing brace of the block that declares it. Since the 2018 edition of Rust, the compiler is more precise: a borrow lasts only until the last line that uses it. This is known as non-lexical lifetimes. The figure marks, for the Vec program, the lines during which f is borrowed and the line that pushes.

With the print last, the push falls inside the borrow and is rejected. With the print moved above the push, the borrow ends at the print and the push is accepted, although the same lines are present. The error was never a matter of which lines exist but of whether a borrow is still going to be used when the conflicting action happens.

afterFigure.text: This makes reordering one of the cheapest repairs for E0502 and E0499. Finish with a reference before changing the value, and the compiler no longer sees a conflict.

steps.headline: Repair the E0502 program by moving lines. Its lines are: 1 let mut v = vec![1];  2 let f = &v[0];  3 v.push(2);  4 println!("{}", f);

workedSteps.text: The borrow f is created on line 2 and last used on line 4, so it is alive across line 3.
The push on line 3 needs a mutable borrow of v while f is still alive, which is the conflict E0502 reports.
Swap lines 3 and 4 so the print comes first. The borrow now ends where f is last used. Count the lines it covers, from the line that creates f to that last use.

reveal.text: The unnamed parameter z could be dropped while the result is still in use, and the compiler allows that because the body cannot return anything borrowed from z.

lessons.orientation: Apply the rule that a value has many shared borrows or one mutable borrow, and annotate a function so a returned reference is tied to its inputs.
lessons.nextAction: Meet C, where none of these rules is checked, and read short fragments that contain the faults Rust prevents.

blocks.text: In C, a program can take the address of the first element of an array stored in a buffer from malloc, the C function that hands out heap memory, and then call realloc, which resizes such a buffer, to make it bigger. If the allocator moves the data to a new block, the old block is freed and the saved address points at memory that belongs to nobody. Nothing in the language stops the program from reading it, and it often appears to work until the day the freed block is reused.

Rust prevents the same situation when the program is compiled. A Vec can grow while a reference into it is held, just as the buffer from malloc can, so the compiler restricts how references to one value may overlap. Those restrictions are what its error messages report, and a reader who knows them can say which one a program breaks and repair it, often by moving a single line.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the rule a borrow error breaks, classify E0502, E0499 and E0597, and write a lifetime annotation that ties a result to its inputs.
intro.whyItMatters: Borrowing is how Rust avoids copying while keeping memory safe, and every Rust program uses it.

recap.keyIdea: A value may have many shared borrows or one mutable borrow, a borrow lasts until its last use, and a lifetime annotation ties a returned reference to the inputs it may borrow from.

blocks.text: The rule that shared and mutable borrows cannot coexist prevents a reference from pointing into a buffer that moves, and the compiler reports a breach as E0502 or E0499. A reference that outlives its value is reported as E0597.

A function that returns a reference must say which inputs it borrows from, and naming a lifetime does so without changing how long any value lives. A borrow ends at its last use, so finishing with a reference before changing the value is the cheapest repair.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to C, where these checks do not exist, and reads short fragments in which the same faults appear.

lessons.title: C pointers and manual memory

lead.text: Memory is a row of numbered bytes, as the first lesson described, and a C variable lives at one of the addresses. The expression `&x` gives the address of `x`, and a variable that can hold such an address is a **pointer**. In `int x = 7; int *p = &x;` the second line declares `p` as a pointer to an `int` and stores the address of `x` in it. The star in front of `p` in an expression, written `*p`, is the reverse operation: it means the object at the address `p` holds.

Because `*p` is that object itself and not a copy of its value, it can stand on the left of an assignment. After `*p = 8` the variable `x` holds 8, though `x` was never named, and a function that receives a pointer can change its caller's variable in this way. A pointer is itself a value of fixed size, 8 bytes on a typical 64-bit target, whatever it points at.

afterFigure.text: Rust's references work in a similar way, with a promise attached. A C pointer carries no promise at all: it may point at freed memory, at nothing, or at the wrong place, and the language does not check.

reveal.text: The assignment changed `x` without naming it, because `*p` and `x` are the same object. A pointer to a pointer works in the same way, one level removed.

lead.text: An array in C is a run of elements side by side, and a pointer to its first element can reach the rest by arithmetic. The expression `q + 1` is the address of the *next element*, so for an `int` pointer, where each `int` occupies four bytes, it is four bytes beyond `q`, and `q + 2` is eight bytes beyond. The compiler scales the offset by the size of the element type so that you never write the byte count yourself.

The subscript is defined in terms of this: `p[i]` is `*(p + i)`, and for an `int` array `p` the element `p[2]` is the `int` at the address eight bytes after `p`. The figure draws three ints in twelve bytes, with the pointer `q` at each of three positions.

afterFigure.text: A common slip is to read `q + 2` as adding two bytes. It adds two elements, and what that is in bytes depends on the type: **the same expression moves an int pointer by eight bytes and a char pointer by two**.

reveal.text: The result is the same element that `p[2]` names, which is why a subscript and a pointer addition are interchangeable in C.

lead.text: Memory on the stack disappears with its frame, so a value that must outlive the function, or whose size is known only while the program runs, needs a block from the heap. In C the request is made by calling `malloc` with a number of bytes, and the result is a pointer to the block. The usual way of stating the size is `sizeof`, which gives a size in bytes: `malloc(sizeof *p)` asks for room for whatever `p` points at, and `malloc(10 * sizeof(int))` asks for ten ints.

Nothing returns the block automatically. When the program has finished with it, it calls `free` with the same pointer, and the block goes back to the allocator. The programmer has to match the calls: a block that is never freed is a *leak*, a block freed twice damages the allocator, and a block used after free is no longer the program's. Nothing in the language records which pointers have been freed, so the pointer `p` still holds its old address after `free(p)`.

afterFigure.text: This is the job that Rust gave to the owner. Where C asks the programmer to remember, Rust's drop frees the block when the owner goes out of scope, once, and the compiler refuses programs that could use it afterwards.

reveal.text: The parameter is a pointer, so the answer is the size of a pointer. gcc warns about this exact mistake with -Wsizeof-array-argument, because it is so common.

lead.text: Where an array is declared, it is an array: `sizeof(arr)` for `int arr[10]` is 40, the full ten elements of four bytes each. In nearly every other use, however, the name of an array is converted to a pointer to its first element, a conversion called **array decay**. Passing the array to a function is such a use, and what the function receives is only the pointer.

A parameter written `int a[]` is therefore not an array at all: the compiler treats it as `int *a`, so inside the function `sizeof(a)` is the size of a pointer, 8 bytes on a typical 64-bit target, and the length of the original array is lost. This is why C functions that take arrays take the length as a separate argument.

afterFigure.text: The practical consequence is that the length has to travel by hand. A function that is given a pointer and the wrong length will happily read or write beyond the array, since nothing in the pointer says where the array ends.

reveal.text: In the scope that declares it, an array knows its size, so dividing `sizeof(arr)` by `sizeof(arr[0])` gives the element count there and only there.

lead.text: A **use after free** reads or writes through a pointer whose block has been freed. A **double free** passes the same block to `free` twice. A **buffer overflow** writes beyond the end of a block, as `p[2]` does to a block with room for two ints. The figure shows each in a few lines of C, with the heap drawn beside it.

All three are **undefined behaviour**, a term of the C standard for code to which the language assigns no meaning at all. The compiler may produce a program that crashes, that appears to work, or that quietly changes a neighbouring variable, and a run that does not crash proves nothing. A buffer overflow that corrupts a neighbour without any visible symptom is more dangerous than one that crashes at once.

afterFigure.text: Tools can find these faults while the program runs. Compiling with gcc or clang and the option `-fsanitize=address` adds AddressSanitizer, which checks every access against a record of the live blocks and stops with a report on the first fault. Rust prevents each of the three: a use after free is E0382 or E0597, a double free cannot be written, and an out-of-range index panics with a message instead of corrupting memory.

steps.headline: Work out the byte distance between q and q + 5 for int p[6] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60}; int *q = p; on a target where an int is 4 bytes.

workedSteps.text: The array starts at address 0x1000, and q holds that address.
Adding 5 to q moves it by five elements, each the size of an int.
Work out the number of bytes between q and q + 5.

reveal.text: Neither a compiler nor the language flags this in C. In Rust the second free is impossible to write, since the owner drops the value only once.

lessons.orientation: Read C pointer arithmetic and array code, and name the memory fault in a short C fragment.
lessons.nextAction: Leave a single program and look at what the operating system provides for it: processes, and the system calls a program makes to use them.

blocks.text: In C, the expression `p[2]` is defined to mean `*(p + 2)`, and nothing in the language checks that the array behind `p` has a third element. The same program that reads its own data correctly with `p[1]` reads whatever happens to lie next in memory with `p[5]`, and the compiler produces code for both without comment.

A pointer is only an address, so a program can add to it, keep using it after its block has been freed, or pass it to a function that has no way to tell how long the array behind it is, and the language checks none of these. Following the arithmetic by hand shows where each pointer lands and which memory fault a fragment commits, and Rust's ownership and borrowing rule out every one of those faults.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to follow pointer arithmetic by hand, say why sizeof gives a different answer inside a function, and name use after free, double free and buffer overflow.
intro.whyItMatters: C code is everywhere under Rust, and reading it is the first step to calling it safely.

recap.keyIdea: A C pointer holds an address and is scaled by element size, an array decays to a pointer when passed on, and nothing checks the memory faults that Rust's rules make impossible.

blocks.text: Adding n to a pointer moves it n elements, so `p[i]` is `*(p + i)`, and an array passed to a function becomes a pointer whose `sizeof` is that of an address. The programmer matches `malloc` with `free`, and a mistake gives a use after free, a double free or a buffer overflow.
These are undefined behaviour, so a run that does not crash proves nothing, and sanitizers such as AddressSanitizer are how C programs check for them while running.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves from one program's memory to the operating system, which runs many programs at once and offers each a way to ask for its services.

lessons.title: Processes and system calls

lead.text: Every program you write runs on top of a single program that is trusted with the machine, the **kernel**. The processor has two privilege levels. In **kernel mode** code may use any instruction and reach any memory or device, and in **user mode** it may not, so a program running in user mode cannot read the disk, send a packet or change another program's memory. Only the kernel runs in kernel mode, and it decides what the other programs may do.

A program that is running, together with the memory and resources the kernel has given it, is a **process**. Each process has its own *address space*, the set of addresses it can use, which the kernel keeps separate from every other process's. The kernel also keeps a record for each process, containing its identification number or **pid**, its open files and its place in the schedule, and it switches between processes so quickly that many appear to run at once.

afterFigure.text: Rust, C and every other language live on the user side of this line. Nothing a program does in its own code can reach beyond it, except by asking the kernel.

lead.text: When a program wants something that only the kernel can do, such as writing text to a terminal, it makes a **system call**. The call `write(1, buf, 5)` asks the kernel to write five bytes, taken from the memory at `buf`, to the file with the number 1, which is the terminal's output. The processor switches to kernel mode, the kernel checks the request and copies the bytes, and it returns the number of bytes written, 5, after which the program carries on in user mode.

The figure steps through this. A system call is much more expensive than an ordinary function call, because of the mode switch, which is why library functions try to make as few as they can. printf is not itself a system call: it is user code that formats text and eventually calls write.

afterFigure.text: This is the whole boundary. Anything a program wants from the machine, a file, a network connection, a new process, more memory or the time, comes as a system call, and so every one of them can be checked, refused or logged by the kernel.

lead.text: The way to start a new process on Unix is the system call `fork`. It duplicates the process that calls it: the new process, called the **child**, starts as a copy of the original, called the **parent**, with the same code, the same variables and the same place in the program, so both continue from the line after the call. Because the two are identical, they need a way to tell themselves apart, and `fork` supplies it by returning a different value in each: the parent receives the child's pid, and the child receives 0.

A program therefore tests the result with an if, and sends the two processes down different branches. The figure shows the parent with pid 100 and a child with pid 101, each with its own copy of the variable x.

afterFigure.text: fork does not start a different program. It makes another copy of the same one, and the copies have separate address spaces, so a change to a variable in one is invisible to the other. The kernel makes this cheap by sharing the pages until one process writes to them and copying only then, a scheme called copy-on-write.

The first fork leaves two processes, and both call the second, which leaves four. Each prints a line, so there are four lines. The next screen shows the doubling at each step.

lead.text: The key fact is that a fork is a line of code like any other, and every process that reaches it runs it. After one fork there are two processes. Each of them reaches the second fork, so each makes a copy, and four processes exist. The third fork is executed by all four, giving eight, so that n forks in a row, with no conditions, leave **2^n processes**.

The figure adds one fork at a time. The original process, P, is joined by a child at each step, but the children are copies and run the same lines, so each of them also forks at the next step. Counting the lines of output of a program that prints once after n forks is the same as counting these boxes.

afterFigure.text: When a fork sits inside an if that tests its own result, only the processes that received that value run the body. That changes the count, and the next screens count such cases.

reveal.text: Five forks give 32 processes and ten give 1024, which is why a loop containing an unconditional fork is called a fork bomb.
A negative result, minus one, would mean that fork failed and no child exists, and a careful program checks for that case too.

lead.text: The **exec** family of system calls replaces the program a process is running. The process keeps its pid and its open files, but its code and data are thrown away and replaced by those of a new program, which starts from the beginning. A call to `exec` does not return when it succeeds, since the code that called it no longer exists. Neither `fork` nor `exec` alone starts a new program in a new process, and Unix combines them. A shell forks, the child calls `exec` to become `ls`, and the shell continues as the parent.

The parent usually calls **wait**, which pauses it until the child exits and then returns the child's exit status. A child that has finished but has not been waited for remains in the process table as a *zombie*, holding only its exit status, until the parent collects it. If the parent does not wait, the order in which the two print is not decided by the program.

afterFigure.text: Splitting the work into fork and exec lets the child change its own surroundings in between, for example by redirecting its output, before the new program starts, which the next lesson uses.

steps.headline: Count the processes after fork(); if (fork() == 0) { fork(); }

workedSteps.text: The first fork runs in the original process and makes a child. Two processes exist, and both go on to the second line.
The second fork is called by both, so each makes a child. Four processes exist. In the two new ones, the second fork returned 0, so only those two run the body of the if.
Each of those two processes forks once more inside the body. Work out the total.

lessons.orientation: Explain what a process is, count the processes that a sequence of forks creates, and say what crosses from user mode to the kernel in a system call.
lessons.nextAction: Follow what a process keeps open, as numbered file descriptors, and see why buffered output can appear more than once after a fork.

blocks.text: In the C line `fork(); fork(); printf("x\n");` there is a single `printf`, yet the program prints more than one line. Each call to `fork` makes a copy of the process that calls it, and the copy carries on from the same place, so the `printf` is run by every process that exists when it is reached.

A process is a running program that the operating system keeps apart from every other one, and creating a new process, like anything else beyond a program's own memory, needs a request to the operating system called a system call. What fork returns in each of the processes it creates decides which lines each one goes on to run, and that is enough to work out by hand how many times a line like this prints.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a process and a system call are, tell parent from child by fork's result, and count the processes after a sequence of forks.
intro.whyItMatters: Processes and system calls explain what a program can and cannot do alone.

recap.keyIdea: A process is a running program with its own address space, and a system call is the one way it asks the kernel for anything, including fork, which makes a copy that returns 0.

blocks.text: The kernel alone runs in kernel mode, so a program that wants a file, a process or the clock makes a system call that crosses into the kernel and back. fork duplicates the caller and returns the child's pid in the parent and 0 in the child, and the copies do not share variables.

Because every existing process runs each fork, n forks in a row create 2^n processes, and a fork inside an if is run only by the processes whose result matches. A shell uses fork, exec and wait to run a command.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at what a process holds open, and why the output of a buffered program can be repeated after a fork.

lessons.title: File descriptors and buffering

lead.text: When a process opens a file, the kernel does not hand over the file. It records the open file in a table belonging to the process and returns the number of the entry, a small non-negative integer called a **file descriptor**. Every later call that reads, writes or closes the file names it by that number, so the program never holds anything but an integer and the kernel keeps everything else.

A process begins with three descriptors already open: 0 is **standard input**, 1 is **standard output** and 2 is **standard error**. The shell normally points all three at the terminal, but that is a choice made for the process and not a property of the numbers. Descriptor 1 is whatever the process was given: a terminal, a file or a pipe, and the program writing to it cannot tell which.

afterFigure.text: A descriptor is not only for files. Terminals, pipes between processes and network connections all appear as descriptors too, which is why one set of calls, read and write, works with all of them.

lead.text: The rule that decides which number a new descriptor gets is simple: the kernel gives the **lowest number that is not in use**. In a process that has only 0, 1 and 2, the first open returns 3, the second 4 and the third 5. If the process then closes 4, that row of the table becomes free, and the next open, which takes the lowest free number, returns 4 again, although 6 would be the next number in sequence.
The figure shows exactly this with four files. Nothing records the history of the numbers, only which rows are in use at this moment.

afterFigure.text: The rule has no exceptions for the standard descriptors. If descriptor 1 has been closed, the next open returns 1, and the program's standard output then goes to that file. The next screen shows how a shell uses this.

diagram.alt: A table of descriptor numbers 0 to 5 beside the objects they refer to. At the start rows 0, 1 and 2 refer to the terminal. Three opens fill 3, 4 and 5. Closing 4 frees that row, and the next open reuses it.

reveal.text: Descriptor numbers are reused, so a number in a log message does not identify a file for long.
Keeping error text on its own descriptor lets a user send normal output to a file and still see the errors on the screen.

lead.text: A shell runs the command `ls > out.txt` with the tools already met. It forks, and in the child it opens `out.txt` and arranges for descriptor 1 to refer to that file, either by closing 1 and opening the file so that the open returns 1, or by calling `dup2`, which makes one descriptor refer to the same object as another. It then calls `exec`, which keeps the descriptor table, and `ls` starts running.

The program ls knows only that it writes its listing to descriptor 1. It prints to the file instead of the terminal without being changed, and without knowing. The figure shows the table of the child before and after the redirection.

afterFigure.text: This is the idea behind the Unix habit of small programs that read descriptor 0 and write descriptor 1: the shell can connect them to files or to each other in any order.

diagram.alt: Two descriptor tables for the command ls. Normally descriptor 1 refers to the terminal. After the shell redirects with > out.txt, descriptor 1 refers to the file out.txt, and the program is unchanged.
diagram.caption: Redirection changes what descriptor 1 refers to, and the program never notices. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: At the fork the text has not been written. It sits in a buffer that the child receives a copy of, and the next screen explains why a terminal behaves differently.

lead.text: `printf` does not `write` immediately. The C library keeps a **buffer** in the process's own memory, adds text to it, and calls the system call write once it holds a lot of text, because one large write is cheaper than many small ones. When the output is a terminal, the library flushes the buffer at every newline so that a person sees lines as they appear. When the output is a file or a pipe, it flushes only when the buffer fills or the program exits.

The buffer lives in the process's address space, and fork copies the address space. A process that forks with unflushed text in its buffer therefore creates a child with the same text in its own buffer, and each flushes its copy later. The figure follows hi through printf, fork and exit when the output is a file.

afterFigure.text: Standard error is the exception: it is unbuffered, so error text is written at once. That is why an error message can appear on the screen before output that was printed earlier, because the earlier output was still waiting in the buffer. Calling `fflush(stdout)` before the fork empties the buffer and removes the repetition.

diagram.alt: A parent process with a buffer holding hi, then a child copy with its own buffer holding hi, then both writing hi into the same file. Without a flush before the fork, the text is in both buffers.
diagram.caption: What happens to unflushed output when a process forks. Use the buttons to step through.

reveal.text: `od -c`, a tool that prints each byte of its input, would show the six characters `h i ! h i !`.

lead.text: Rust's standard output keeps a buffer that is flushed at each newline, so `print!` with no newline may wait while `println!` does not. A `BufWriter` wraps any writer in a larger buffer of your own, which gathers many small writes into few, and it must be flushed, either by calling `flush` or by dropping the `BufWriter`. The program in the figure writes two lines through a `BufWriter` and flushes it.

At the bottom of every one of these layers is the system call `write(fd, buf, n)`, which has no buffer in the process at all: the bytes go to the kernel immediately. `printf`, `println!` and `BufWriter` are all ways of making fewer calls to it.

afterFigure.text: Because Rust has no fork in its standard library, the doubled output is a C problem for the most part, but the same ordering effects appear whenever buffered output and standard error are mixed.

steps.headline: Follow the descriptors: open A, open B, open C, close A, close C, open D, open E.

workedSteps.text: A, B and C are opened with 0, 1 and 2 already in use, so they get the three lowest free numbers.
Closing A and C frees 3 and 5, and B keeps 4.
D takes the lowest free number, which is 3. Work out the number E receives.

reveal.text: A program started with 0 closed would find that its first open becomes its standard input without the program asking. Shells rely on exactly this, deliberately.

lessons.orientation: Predict descriptor numbers after opens and closes, and predict how often output repeats when a buffered process forks.
lessons.nextAction: Run several lines of execution inside one process, sharing memory, and see what that sharing allows to go wrong.

blocks.text: The two lines `printf("hi\n"); fork();` print `hi` once when the program runs at a terminal, yet with its output sent to a file the same program prints it a different number of times, although the source has not changed. The difference lies in where the text waits before it leaves the process, and in what the process uses to refer to its output at all.

Both come down to the file descriptor, the small number by which a process names everything it has open, and to the way the C library collects text before writing it. Between them they explain how many times a line appears after a fork, and what a shell changes when it redirects a program's output to a file.

diagram.alt: The same two lines of C run twice. At a terminal the output is the line hi once. When the output goes to a file, the line hi appears twice.
diagram.caption: The same program with two destinations for its output. Use the buttons to compare.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a descriptor is, predict the number that open returns after closes, and predict whether buffered output appears twice after a fork.
intro.whyItMatters: Descriptors and buffering explain redirection, pipes and the odd repeated line.

recap.keyIdea: A descriptor is a small number that refers to an open object, open returns the lowest free one, and text that is still in a buffer at a fork is written by both processes.

blocks.text: A new process has descriptors 0, 1 and 2 for input, output and error, and each open returns the lowest number that is free, so closed numbers are reused. A shell redirects a program by changing what descriptor 1 refers to before the program runs.

printf keeps text in a buffer that is flushed at each newline on a terminal but only when full or at exit for a file or pipe, so a fork with text in the buffer gives the child a copy of it, and the text is written twice.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson puts several threads of execution inside one process, where memory is shared and updates can be lost.

lessons.title: Threads and shared state

lead.text: The previous lessons treated a process as one stream of execution with memory of its own. A process can contain several, called **threads**, each with its own stack and its own position in the code. All the threads of a process see the same address space, so a value on the heap, or a global, written by one thread can be read by another at once, without a pipe or any copy.

The figure sets this beside two separate processes. Shared memory is the reason to use threads, since splitting a job over several processors is far easier when the pieces can reach the same data, and it is also the hazard, because two threads can now touch the same data at the same time.

afterFigure.text: A thread is cheaper to create than a process for the same reason: there is no new address space to build. The cost is that the isolation the kernel gave each process is gone, and the program itself has to keep its threads from interfering.

diagram.alt: Two views. Two processes each have their own memory and one thread. One process with two threads has one shared memory block, with each thread keeping its own stack and registers.
diagram.caption: Threads share a process's memory, and processes do not. Use the buttons to compare.
